routes.description: Establish that Christianity can coherently recognize suffering as genuinely wrong within a broken creation while relating it to human freedom, divine presence, justice, and promised restoration.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the framework explains why suffering is real evil without requiring a purpose for every tragedy, preserves divine goodness and power, and connects present brokenness to morally adequate divine action and future healing.

motionBridge.description: Show that the Christian account makes coherent overall sense of suffering alongside an all-powerful and all-loving God.

centralBridges.description: Explain how a good creation can be presently broken and why its natural mechanisms can produce suffering without making suffering morally illusory.
Account for divine love through God's presence with sufferers, participation in suffering, and action against evil rather than through a distinct benefit assigned to every tragedy.
Show how resurrection, judgment, forgiveness, and future restoration can heal suffering and put wrongs right without disregarding victims or consequences.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Ground the judgment that suffering and exploitation are objectively wrong rather than merely evolutionarily disfavored.
Explain the roles of consequential human freedom and incomplete present healing within the wider broken-world framework.

routes.description: Establish that suffering is expected under naturalism but creates unresolved tensions among divine omnipotence, perfect love, selective intervention, judgment, and the claimed final defeat of evil.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if apparently gratuitous suffering and the Christian framework's treatment of healing and salvation remain less compatible with an all-powerful, all-loving God than with naturalistic expectations.

motionBridge.description: Show that the observed reality and distribution of suffering make belief in the specified Christian God unreasonable.

centralBridges.description: Establish why an omnipotent and perfectly loving God would need a morally sufficient account of every evil that God knowingly permits.
Show that natural processes can explain suffering and human aversion to it without invoking divine purposes or transcendent moral explanation.
Test whether selective and ambiguous recoveries provide evidence of divine intervention rather than outcomes expected from natural uncertainty.
Determine whether judgment based on belief or reconciliation treats sincere unbelief and grave wrongdoing consistently with perfect love and proportionate justice.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Examine whether changing Christian moral practice weakens the claimed explanatory advantage of an objective divine standard.
Assess whether promised resurrection and future healing are sufficiently warranted to resolve rather than postpone the evidential problem.

sections.title: Suffering, naturalism, and the coherence of a broken creation
sections.rationale: This section contains the motion's foundational clash over whether naturalism adequately accommodates suffering or whether Christian broken-creation claims better explain both its mechanisms and its status as a genuine wrong.

sections.title: Evolution, objective morality, and human dignity
sections.rationale: The competing accounts of moral aversion, cooperation, objective norms, and equal dignity bear on whether Christianity supplies explanatory resources that naturalism lacks and whether its historical record affects that claim.

sections.title: Divine presence, permitted evil, and future restoration
sections.rationale: The issue tests whether divine solidarity, epistemic limits, resurrection, and eventual healing can reconcile perfect goodness with permitted atrocities, or whether every permitted evil still demands an adequate greater-good justification.

sections.title: Unanswered prayer and evidence of divine healing
sections.rationale: Selective recovery provides a concrete test of the broken-world and partially realized kingdom account against the contention that natural uncertainty predicts the observed pattern better than purposeful divine intervention.

sections.title: Judgment, forgiveness, freedom, and sincere unbelief
sections.rationale: This section examines whether divine judgment, costly forgiveness, human freedom, and an inclusive invitation can secure justice for victims while treating sincere unbelievers and repentant wrongdoers consistently with perfect love.

moves.speaker: Stephen Woodford
moves.proposition: Naturalism accommodates suffering as part of nature, whereas divine omnipotence and perfect love imply that every apparently evil event must contribute to a greater good.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly turns to Stephen, and the sustained first-person atheist answer occupies the window until the moderator resumes.

response.rationale: This constructive move establishes the initial naturalistic contrast and the claimed greater-good tension without answering an earlier locked move.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly establishes the foundational contrast and the principal challenge for the opposing framework.

precisionFindings.rationale: The contrast is recoverable, but the universal claim that every evil must yield a greater good lacks an explicit doctrinal or logical qualification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move asserts a necessary greater-good implication, although omnipotence and love alone do not establish that exact formulation without further premises.

charity.alternative: A loving God may oppose evil while permitting some evil for freedom, stable natural order, or reasons not reducible to a benefit from each event.
charity.decisiveQualification: The move does not show that perfect love logically requires a distinct greater good produced by every individual evil.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The naturalism contrast is intelligible, but the inference from divine attributes to a greater good for every evil leaves a substantial conditional unsupported.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move supplies a clear conceptual contrast but no defended warrant or alternative comparison establishing its universal greater-good premise.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the con motion bridge by arguing that suffering creates a foundational inconsistency for the specified God.

representationalCharity.rationale: It identifies a serious problem but frames the Christian alternative too narrowly around a benefit assigned to every event.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says naturalism has no theological evil-explanation problem and expressly claims that Christianity must understand evil as serving a greater good.

moves.speaker: Sharon Dirckx
moves.proposition: The Christian account of a good but broken creation explains both suffering's natural mechanisms and humanity's conviction that suffering is genuinely wrong.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator asks Sharon directly, and the ensuing extended answer uses her scientific background before the moderator addresses Stephen.

components.text: Whether Christianity can make coherent sense of suffering as real wrongness rather than a theological anomaly.
Whether every evil must be shown to contribute to a particular greater good.

response.rationale: The move contacts the broad coherence challenge by presenting beautiful-but-broken creation and genuine wrongness, but it does not answer the opponent's universal permission inference.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This is a partial answer that contacts the foundational coherence component while leaving the decisive every-evil inference unresolved.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposition is clear, though the causal content of a world being 'broken' remains only partly specified in the selected evidence.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move presents the framework as sense-making rather than as a demonstrated exclusive explanation, with one implicit causal qualification.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The good-but-broken distinction coherently permits natural suffering to be genuinely wrong, but the mechanism connecting divine goodness to brokenness is compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The excerpt supports the stated framework and phenomenological wrongness, but largely asserts rather than defends the broken-creation explanation.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It reaches the indispensable broken-creation bridge by explaining how natural mechanisms and genuine moral wrongness coexist.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move develops its own Christian account without materially characterizing or testing a rival interpretation of the opposing argument.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly says the Christian framework validates suffering's wrongness and describes the world as simultaneously beautiful and broken.

moves.speaker: Stephen Woodford
moves.proposition: Evolutionary selection explains widespread aversion to suffering and the social impulse to improve conditions through dispositions favoring survival, reproduction, longevity, and prosperity.
moves.attributionBasis: Stephen begins after Sharon asks for naturalistic grounds, answers in a sustained first-person explanation, and yields when Sharon responds.

components.text: Whether widespread human recognition and avoidance of suffering requires the Christian broken-world framework.

response.rationale: The evolutionary account directly offers a naturalistic explanation of aversion to suffering, though it does not address the Christian claim about objective wrongness itself.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the explanatory component decisively but leaves the distinct normative-status component of the earlier move unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The evolutionary explanation is recoverable and stable, with the ordinary implicit qualification that selection explains dispositions rather than every judgment.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claimed evolutionary pathway fits the limited explanatory aim, although its population-level and dispositional scope is left implicit.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Natural selection coherently explains inherited aversive and social dispositions, with only a bounded implicit bridge from fitness effects to current intuitions.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The account invokes well-known evolutionary mechanisms and animal aversion, but compresses the empirical support and rival-explanation comparison.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the central naturalistic-explanation bridge by supplying a non-theistic account of aversion to suffering.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move offers an independent causal explanation and does not rely on a substantive portrayal of the strongest Christian alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt invokes natural selection, inherited social dispositions, and widespread avoidance of suffering among humans and nonhuman animals.

moves.speaker: Sharon Dirckx
moves.proposition: Evolution may explain how moral dispositions arise, but it cannot determine why compassionate norms are objectively better than exploitative survival strategies.
moves.attributionBasis: Sharon takes the floor in direct acknowledgment of Stephen's evolutionary account and develops the counterargument until Stephen announces his rejoinder.

components.text: Whether explaining the evolutionary origin of moral dispositions also establishes which resulting moral norms are objectively better.
Whether naturalism can explain the objective wrongness attributed to suffering.

response.rationale: The move expressly diagnoses the descriptive-to-normative gap and states that selection could support incompatible strategies without ranking them objectively.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly identifies the inference it rejects and states the defeating consequence for the naturalistic moral explanation.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between causal origins and objective normative ranking is explicit, stable, and scoped to what evolution alone can determine.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The limited claim that a selection mechanism alone does not normatively rank possible strategies matches the conceptual warrant offered.

charity.alternative: Evolutionary naturalists may combine evolved dispositions with independent moral reasoning rather than derive all normativity from selection itself.
charity.decisiveQualification: The move's criticism succeeds only against the claim that evolutionary mechanism by itself supplies objective ranking.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The is-to-ought distinction is clearly applied, though the further suggestion that the external standard points toward God remains a bounded unsupported bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The contrasting survival strategies illustrate the conceptual gap, but the positive inference toward God lacks developed comparative support.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the subsidiary moral-grounding bridge by challenging selection as a complete source of objective moral ranking.

representationalCharity.rationale: The wording focuses on the mechanism itself and therefore substantially preserves, though does not develop, the strongest naturalistic alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt states that different moral apparatuses could aid survival and that the evolutionary mechanism itself cannot say which is better.

moves.speaker: Stephen Woodford
moves.proposition: Cooperation can be evolutionarily advantageous, while changing Christian treatment of women and slavery weakens the claim that Christianity uniquely supplies unchanging objective moral guidance.
moves.attributionBasis: Stephen explicitly introduces his rejoinder, develops both evolutionary and historical objections, and stops as Sharon begins her answer.

components.text: Whether natural processes can favor cooperation and thereby explain compassionate moral dispositions without an external divine standard.
Whether Christianity in practice provides stable and uniquely objective moral guidance.
Whether Christianity uniquely validates judgments that suffering and exclusion are wrong.

response.rationale: The reply contacts both cooperation and the asserted advantage of Christian moral guidance, using historical moral change as a separate counterexample.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It gives substantial direct contact to both decisive components of the immediately preceding moral-grounding argument.

precisionFindings.rationale: Both strands are recoverable, but references to what 'the Christian' must conclude generalize across diverse doctrines and historical positions.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Historical moral change supports a challenge to unique guidance, but the implied dilemma about God changing or believers being wrong is somewhat compressed.

charity.alternative: Christians may distinguish an unchanging moral foundation from fallible and historically changing human interpretations of it.
charity.decisiveQualification: Changing Christian practice does not by itself prove that the underlying standard changed, though it weakens claims of uniquely clear guidance.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The evolutionary cooperation point and historical counterexample are coherent, but the proposed dilemma for objective divine morality is not exhaustive.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Women and slavery are material historical examples, though documentation, representativeness, and comparison with doctrinal resources remain compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It reaches the subsidiary moral-history bridge directly by testing Christianity's claimed advantage through changing moral practice.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move notes historical development effectively but underplays the live distinction between doctrine and fallible interpretation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The selected span appeals to expanding empathy and changing Christian judgments, while the full locked proposition also advances evolutionary cooperation.

moves.speaker: Sharon Dirckx
moves.proposition: Christianity grounds equal human dignity in creation and Jesus's conduct even though later Christian authorities sometimes failed to follow that mandate.
moves.attributionBasis: Sharon begins by qualifying Stephen's account and continues through a focused defense of Genesis and Jesus before the moderator intervenes.

components.text: Whether Christianity contains foundational resources for equal dignity despite later Christian failures and changing practices.
Whether historical Christian authorities consistently implemented those resources.

response.rationale: The reply directly distinguishes foundational teachings from failures of implementation and cites creation and Jesus as the proposed equal-dignity basis.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the historical objection and supplies a clear doctrinal explanation of why later failures need not negate the foundation.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move explicitly limits its defense by acknowledging later Christian failure while identifying the claimed foundation of equal dignity.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conclusion that Christianity contains equal-dignity resources fits the cited Genesis teaching and the express historical qualification.

charity.alternative: Christian texts and institutions have also been interpreted to sustain hierarchy, slavery, and unequal treatment.
charity.decisiveQualification: Foundational egalitarian passages show resources for equality but do not establish consistent historical guidance or erase contrary interpretations.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Distinguishing foundational mandate from later noncompliance is coherent and directly avoids the inference that abuse disproves the stated norm.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Genesis, the surrounding ancient context, and Jesus's conduct provide specific support, with a bounded gap concerning competing historical interpretations.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary moral-grounding bridge by locating equal dignity in creation and exemplary Christian teaching.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly acknowledges institutional failure, though it does not examine contrary texts or the persistence of competing interpretations.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts ancient assertions of female inferiority with Genesis's claim that male and female alike bear God's image and equal value.

moves.speaker: Sharon Dirckx
moves.proposition: Christianity treats evil as genuinely wrong without requiring each tragedy to be God's will, divine punishment, or a means to a particular benefit.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator asks Sharon for her response, and she gives a continuous answer until the transition to Stephen's interjection.

components.text: Whether Christianity is committed to treating every tragedy as God's will or as a means producing a particular greater good.
Whether Christianity can classify suffering as genuinely evil and wrong.

response.rationale: The reply expressly rejects the assumed commitment and states the consequence: Christianity may condemn an event as evil without assigning it a specific divine purpose.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly identifies and rejects the central greater-good framing while affirmatively explaining the framework's contrary classification.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between divine will, resulting good, and genuinely operative evil is explicit and consistently limited to particular tragedies.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move confidently states what the offered Christian framework need not claim, and the supplied distinction matches that bounded conclusion.

charity.alternative: The opponent's deeper claim concerns God's knowing permission of evil, not merely whether Christians verbally call each event God's will.
charity.decisiveQualification: Rejecting a purpose per tragedy does not yet explain how perfect love is compatible with knowingly permitting purposeless evil.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction coherently blocks an inference from divine sovereignty to each evil being willed, though permission remains insufficiently explained.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move clearly states the framework but relies mainly on doctrinal assertion and does not defend how divine power relates to operative evil.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly attacks the central permission-of-evil bridge by denying that each permitted tragedy requires a specific beneficial purpose.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply accurately rejects one formulation but does not fully engage the stronger permission-based version of the objection.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says evil is real, rejects describing each tragedy as God's will, and depicts good and evil as both active in a broken world.

moves.speaker: Stephen Woodford
moves.proposition: Because an omnipotent and perfectly loving God knowingly permits each evil, Christianity must hold that even apparently gratuitous suffering and atrocities contribute to a superior outcome.
moves.attributionBasis: Stephen signals his interjection and restates his logical argument in a continuous passage before Sharon begins her disagreement.

components.text: Whether rejecting a purpose for each tragedy answers the problem created by God's omnipotence and knowing permission of every evil.
Whether calling creation broken explains why an omnipotent God permits its harmful operation.
Whether objective human dignity resolves divine permission of suffering.

response.rationale: The reply directly shifts from whether evil is called God's will to the stronger inference from omnipotence, permission, and love, though its greater-good conclusion remains underargued.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the decisive permission issue and explains why merely labeling evil as wrong does not discharge it.

precisionFindings.rationale: The permission argument is clearly recoverable, but the move omits the qualification that moral permission can be justified without each evil producing a superior outcome.

calibrationFindings.rationale: God's ability and permission generate a demand for sufficient reason, but they do not alone entail that every evil contributes to a superior outcome.

charity.alternative: A morally sufficient reason may concern freedom, regular natural order, or constraints on intervention without making the evil itself productive of greater good.
charity.decisiveQualification: The argument must distinguish a sufficient reason for permission from the stronger claim that each evil contributes to a better outcome.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from omnipotent permission to a need for justification is strong, but the further universal greater-good conclusion is a substantial unsupported conditional.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move supplies vivid examples and a conceptual premise but does not defend its necessity claim against alternative sufficient-reason accounts.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central permission-of-evil bridge by focusing on knowing divine permission under omnipotence and perfect love.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move presses the strongest permission question but collapses distinct forms of justification into a universal greater-good requirement.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt argues that an all-powerful God can prevent anything and therefore permits every existing evil, then asks why such permission occurs.

moves.speaker: Sharon Dirckx
moves.proposition: Some atrocities are unqualified evils rather than necessary means to greater goods, while human inability to identify all divine reasons does not establish that none exist.
moves.attributionBasis: Sharon begins with an explicit disagreement, develops the distinction between evil and resulting good, and completes her epistemic point as the moderator moves on.

components.text: Whether every permitted atrocity must itself produce a greater good in order for divine goodness to remain coherent.
Whether inability to identify a divine reason establishes that no morally sufficient reason exists.
Whether Christianity must redescribe atrocities as beneficial parts of a plan.

response.rationale: The move rejects a benefit from atrocities and invokes epistemic limits against inferring that no reason exists, but it does not supply an affirmative sufficient reason for permission.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts both decisive demands, yet the answer remains materially incomplete because possibility of unknown reasons does not establish their adequacy.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is recoverable and explicitly limited, although 'reasons' ranges between reasons for permission and goods resulting from evil.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The epistemic claim is appropriately modest: human inability to identify all reasons does not demonstrate that none can exist.

charity.alternative: The evidential objection need not claim certainty that no reason exists; it can argue that apparently gratuitous evil lowers the probability of perfect divine love.
charity.decisiveQualification: Merely possible unknown reasons answer a deductive inference more effectively than a probabilistic evidential challenge.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between evil and later good is coherent, but combining categorical condemnation with unknown divine reasons leaves the permission account underdeveloped.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Historical atrocities support the claim that some evils should not be called beneficial, while the unknown-reasons defense remains largely speculative.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central permission bridge by denying the universal greater-good requirement and limiting the epistemic inference.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly recognizes the demand for reasons but responds mainly to a stronger certainty claim than the best evidential objection requires.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt calls genocide and the Holocaust abject evil with no greater good produced, while the locked proposition adds the limited unknown-reasons point.

moves.speaker: Sharon Dirckx
moves.proposition: Christianity answers suffering through a God who entered history and suffered in Jesus, remains present with sufferers, and promises resurrection and eventual healing.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly directs the Christian-worldview question to Sharon, and the uninterrupted answer uses first-person Christian testimony consistent with her position.

components.text: Whether divine love must be defended by assigning a benefit to each permitted tragedy rather than by God's opposition, solidarity, and restoration.
Whether Christianity offers a coherent positive response to suffering beyond explaining its causal occurrence.
Whether evolutionary aversion explains divine presence with sufferers.
Whether historical moral change defeats Christian claims about divine solidarity.

response.rationale: The move justifies a replacement demand centered on God's participation in suffering, present help, and eventual healing, preserving the issue of loving divine response without requiring a benefit per event.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reframe is explicit and supplies a substantial positive response, though it does not fully explain why preventable suffering is initially permitted.

precisionFindings.rationale: The three-part response of incarnation, presence, and promised restoration is clearly recoverable and distinguished from a purpose assigned to each tragedy.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move presents experiential presence and future restoration as a coherent answer, but the testimony and promise do not independently establish their truth.

charity.alternative: Divine solidarity and future repair may matter morally while still failing to justify an omnipotent God's prior permission of preventable suffering.
charity.decisiveQualification: Participation and compensation address response and restoration more directly than the original permission decision.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Solidarity, presence, and restoration form a coherent divine-response account, with a bounded but important gap concerning antecedent permission.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move cites Christian narrative, Psalms, and personal experience, but the resurrection and future-healing claims lack independent support here.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the central divine-response bridge through incarnation, present solidarity, and action oriented toward restoration.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move preserves the seriousness of suffering and offers a substantial answer, though the strongest permission objection remains distinct.

moves.evidenceBasis: The selected evidence describes God as present help and reports personal experience, while the locked span also invokes Jesus's suffering and promised resurrection.

moves.speaker: Stephen Woodford
moves.proposition: Christian promises of future healing merit skepticism, and restricting their benefit to believers would treat sincere unbelievers incompatibly with the perfect love attributed to God.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator asks whether heaven is a helpful fiction, after which Stephen gives a sustained skeptical analogy and explicitly speaks from the atheist position.

components.text: Whether promised resurrection and future healing are warranted and whether their benefits extend consistently to sincere unbelievers.
Whether future hope can resolve atrocities whose present justification remains unknown.
Whether calling tragedies purposeless answers the justice of their ultimate outcome.

response.rationale: The reply directly questions both the warrant for future healing and the compatibility of exclusive salvation with perfect love, although the evidence excerpt develops exclusion more than warrant.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive future-restoration claim and adds a direct moral test concerning sincere nonbelievers.

precisionFindings.rationale: The skeptical challenge is clear, but it groups Christianity and Islam and treats contested exclusivist teachings as if they uniformly define each tradition.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The moral concern is well motivated, but the move overgeneralizes from particular exclusivist interpretations without acknowledging doctrinal variation.

charity.alternative: Christian accounts may include inclusivism, postmortem reconciliation, or judgment sensitive to knowledge and sincere response rather than simple propositional belief.
charity.decisiveQualification: The objection is strongest against strict belief-conditioned exclusion, not against every Christian account of judgment and restoration.

logicalCoherence.rationale: If strict belief-conditioned exclusion is assumed, the love tension follows coherently, but that crucial doctrinal premise is insufficiently qualified.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move identifies recognizable teachings and a serious moral comparison, but supplies little support for uniform exclusivity or its exact conditions.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central salvation-justice bridge by testing sincere unbelief against perfect love and promised final healing.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move raises a powerful qualification but presents the strict exclusivist version too readily as the uniform Christian position.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt questions whether atheists receive promised salvation and cites teachings that condition heaven on belief, then asks what a good God would do.

moves.speaker: Sharon Dirckx
moves.proposition: Final judgment expresses divine love because God knows every heart, corrects earthly injustice, opposes evil, and extends an inclusive invitation to reconciliation.
moves.attributionBasis: The response adopts the Christian first-person plural and directly develops Sharon's recurring claims about ultimate justice, divine love, and an open invitation to God.

components.text: Whether divine judgment and reconciliation can treat persons lovingly and justly rather than excluding sincere unbelievers mechanically.
Whether future restoration is evidentially warranted rather than merely asserted.
Whether ultimate justice constitutes an adequate response to permitted evil.

response.rationale: The reply contacts the moral-exclusion concern through divine knowledge of hearts and a radically inclusive invitation, but it does not answer the warrant challenge or specify unbelievers' outcomes.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive moral component but leaves the scope and conditions of salvation materially unresolved.

precisionFindings.rationale: Judgment, love, and invitation are clear, but 'radically inclusive' does not specify the actual conditions or outcomes for sincere unbelievers.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move confidently asserts perfect divine knowledge and ultimate justice while leaving their operation and the exclusion question insufficiently qualified.

charity.alternative: An invitation can be formally open yet remain inaccessible to people who sincerely lack sufficient evidence for belief.
charity.decisiveQualification: Inclusiveness of invitation does not alone establish fairness of outcomes or answer involuntary unbelief.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Love, opposition to evil, and judgment can coherently coexist, but the bridge from inclusive invitation to fair treatment of unbelief remains material.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move states central Christian doctrines clearly but offers assertion rather than specific support for perfect heart-reading or ultimate rectification.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the central restoration-justice bridge by connecting judgment, concern for victims, reconciliation, and divine love.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply recognizes the love concern but does not address the strongest distinction between an open offer and a genuinely accessible one.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says God cares about evil, will ultimately bring justice, knows people in love, and offers a radically inclusive invitation.

moves.speaker: Sharon Dirckx
moves.proposition: Unanswered healing prayer reflects a broken world in which God's kingdom has begun but is incomplete, so non-healing implies neither deficient faith nor divine punishment.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator addresses Sharon by name, and her uninterrupted answer explains Jesus' healings, Christian prayer, and the unfinished kingdom from an explicitly Christian standpoint.

components.text: Whether incomplete present healing can fit the Christian framework without making failed prayer punishment or deficient faith.
Whether non-healing has a distinct beneficial purpose in every case.
Whether broken creation generally explains the observed distribution of suffering.

response.rationale: The move directly explains non-healing within an inaugurated but incomplete kingdom and rejects punitive or faith-deficiency interpretations, while not providing a selection principle for healing.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the relevant theological demands clearly, but the observed selectivity of healing remains unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move clearly distinguishes begun from completed kingdom and explicitly rules out several claimed implications of unanswered prayer.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The account is internally coherent and qualified, although brokenness alone does not explain why particular prayers receive different outcomes.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The already-not-yet framework consistently permits incomplete healing and rejects blame, but it lacks a bridge explaining selective intervention.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Appeal to Jesus's healings and doctrinal structure gives some support, while the explanation of actual differential outcomes remains asserted.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary freedom-prayer bridge by locating unanswered prayer within incomplete present restoration.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move primarily clarifies its own doctrine of unanswered prayer rather than characterizing a developed opposing explanation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly denies inadequate faith, insufficient prayer, and punishment as explanations, instead attributing non-healing to continuing brokenness.

moves.speaker: Stephen Woodford
moves.proposition: Natural uncertainty can explain selective surprising recoveries, whereas genuine divine healing should also produce clear outcomes such as restored limbs rather than only ambiguous remissions.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly turns to Stephen, whose answer contrasts atheist naturalism with the Christian healing account and presents a sustained skeptical test for miracles.

components.text: Whether the broken-world explanation distinguishes selective recoveries from outcomes already expected under natural medical uncertainty.
Whether divine healing should produce unambiguous outcomes outside ordinary remission patterns.
Whether experiential divine presence independently establishes intervention in healing.
Whether eventual justice explains current selective recoveries.

response.rationale: The move expressly diagnoses the evidential indistinguishability problem and states a defeating expectation: genuine intervention should include clear outcomes such as restored limbs.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly attacks the explanatory inference, supplies a natural rival, and states a concrete discriminating prediction.

precisionFindings.rationale: The evidential test is clear, though claims that healings are always vague and limited to self-resolving conditions are broader than the support shown.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The comparative prediction is forceful and testable, but categorical language about all reported healings exceeds the excerpt's evidential base.

charity.alternative: A theist may expect rare, non-coercive, or medically mediated healing rather than uniformly spectacular violations of ordinary biological patterns.
charity.decisiveQualification: Such expectations can reduce the force of the limb-restoration test but also make intervention harder to distinguish from natural outcomes.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The rival-explanation comparison and demand for discriminating evidence are coherent, with one bounded assumption about what divine healing should look like.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Cancer remission and absent limb restoration are specific evidential contrasts, though frequencies and representative documentation are not supplied.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central healing-evidence bridge by comparing selective recovery with natural uncertainty and a concrete miracle prediction.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move uses a strong discriminating test while leaving some room, implicitly, for natural uncertainty and varying expected miracle models.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts conditions that sometimes remit naturally with the absence of restored limbs and other obvious signs expected from miraculous intervention.

moves.speaker: Stephen Woodford
moves.proposition: Sincere unbelievers cannot force conviction in weak religious claims, so eternally punishing earnest nonbelief is inconsistent with an all-loving God who controls the salvific system.
moves.attributionBasis: Following an audience question about atheists and heaven, the speaker identifies himself as an atheist and develops Stephen's established objection to hell and involuntary disbelief.

components.text: Whether a radically inclusive invitation is genuinely accessible when sincere people cannot voluntarily make themselves believe weakly evidenced claims.
Whether eternal treatment of earnest unbelief is proportionate and compatible with perfect love.
Whether promised restoration encompasses sincere unbelievers.
Whether unanswered prayer contributes to reasonable nonbelief.

response.rationale: The reply directly challenges accessibility, voluntariness, and proportionality, turning the inclusive-invitation claim into a concrete test involving earnest nonbelief.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the decisive premise that invitation is inclusive and explains why involuntary disbelief creates a contrary consequence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The sincere-unbelief argument is clear, but eternal punishment and belief-based judgment are treated as uniform Christian commitments without doctrinal qualification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The incompatibility claim is strong under strict exclusivism, but its unqualified application to the offered Christian framework is somewhat overstated.

charity.alternative: Judgment may account for available evidence, motives, character, and response to truth rather than punish mere inability to assent to a proposition.
charity.decisiveQualification: If judgment is individualized in that way, sincere unbelief alone need not generate the asserted eternal penalty.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Given belief-conditioned eternal punishment, involuntary sincere unbelief creates a clear love tension, but the doctrinal conditional remains material.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The phenomenology of inability to force conviction is plausibly stated, while the exact salvific policy and eternal consequence are insufficiently established.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central salvation-justice bridge by testing sincere nonbelief against perfect love and proportional judgment.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move powerfully presents involuntary disbelief but insufficiently engages the preceding claim that God knows each heart.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt describes an earnest seeker unable to become convinced and asks whether an all-loving God would mistreat that person eternally.

moves.speaker: Sharon Dirckx
moves.proposition: Christian forgiveness does not erase justice: Christ bears evil at great cost, victims remain seen, perpetrators face consequences, and reconciliation includes transformation.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator asks Sharon to respond, and the long uninterrupted answer consistently presents Christian doctrines of justice, sin, atonement, forgiveness, and moral transformation.

components.text: Whether Christian reconciliation and forgiveness can preserve justice for victims and consequences for perpetrators.
Whether sincere unbelievers are punished merely for inability to believe.
Whether salvation is restricted to belief in a morally arbitrary way.
Whether ultimate restoration disregards the cost and reality of evil.
Whether present healing claims are evidentially distinguishable.

response.rationale: The move answers the justice-for-victims and cheap-forgiveness concern in detail, but it does not contact the primary sincere-unbelief demand that immediately motivates the salvation objection.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts a significant secondary justice component while leaving the decisive involuntary-unbelief component unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: Costly forgiveness, victim recognition, perpetrator consequences, and transformation are clearly distinguished, with explicit acknowledgment of limited understanding.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move advocates the internal coherence of costly forgiveness while expressly acknowledging uncertainty about the details of final judgment.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Cost-bearing atonement, consequences, victim recognition, and transformation coherently distinguish forgiveness from costless acquittal, with details left implicit.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move specifies the doctrinal mechanisms but relies on asserted Christian commitments rather than independently supporting their operation or outcomes.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the central restoration-justice bridge by explaining how forgiveness can retain cost, consequences, and regard for victims.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move develops a positive account of atonement and justice without materially depicting a rival theory in a way that permits a charity test.

moves.evidenceBasis: The locked span says Christ bears evil at cost, victims remain seen, perpetrators face justice, and reconciliation involves moral transformation.

moves.speaker: Stephen Woodford
moves.proposition: A system that may save a sincerely converted genocidal offender while condemning a decent but unconvinced atheist reverses proportionate moral outcomes and conflicts with a good God.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator gives the remaining seconds to Stephen, who directly criticizes Sharon's preceding answer and contrasts the fates of a genocidal convert and an unconvinced atheist.

components.text: Whether costly forgiveness and transformation prevent salvation from yielding disproportionate outcomes between grave offenders and decent unbelievers.
Whether a radically inclusive invitation produces morally proportionate final judgment.
Whether promised restoration is distributed consistently with perfect love.
Whether epistemic limitations excuse sincere nonbelief.

response.rationale: The reply directly alleges a reversed moral outcome and contrasts a converted genocidal offender with a decent unconvinced atheist, but assumes rather than establishes each final fate.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the justice claim and presents a concrete counterexample aimed at its proportionality.

precisionFindings.rationale: The comparison is vivid and recoverable, but 'saved,' 'punished,' and sincere conversion lack specified conditions, and the doctrinal scope is generalized.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move asserts definite outcomes for two stylized cases although the preceding account emphasized heart knowledge, transformation, consequences, and uncertainty.

charity.alternative: Genuine repentance may require transformation and does not erase consequences, while sincere unbelief may be judged according to knowledge and motives rather than automatically condemned.
charity.decisiveQualification: The asymmetry follows only if last-minute assent guarantees salvation and decent nonbelief guarantees punishment regardless of heart or conduct.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The moral comparison would be forceful under the assumed rules, but those rules conflict with qualifications in the immediately preceding account and remain unsupported.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The hypothetical illustrates a concern but supplies no evidence that the offered framework guarantees either stipulated final outcome.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central salvation-justice bridge by testing proportional outcomes for grave wrongdoing and sincere unbelief.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection identifies a serious possible asymmetry but weakens the preceding account by reducing transformation to deathbed assent.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts a genocidal person professing Christianity at death with an atheist who is not bad but remains unconvinced.
